fields.about: Mean-field and shell-model calculations of nuclei.
fields.overview:
Nuclear structure two ways.
- Skyrme Hartree-Fock, the mean field of a spherical nucleus
- the shell model, configuration interaction in a valence space
The shell model is checked against BIGSTICK.

nuclear.shell_model.summary: The lowest states of a nucleus in the nuclear shell model: Z valence protons and N valence neutrons outside a closed core, in one of the shipped spaces (the sd shell with USDB, the p shell with Cohen-Kurath), or in a .sps and .int pair read from disk. lib/nuclear/shell/shell.viv builds the M-scheme basis and applies H; lib/eigen/lowest finds the states with Lanczos (or, by `eigensolver`, from H as a matrix); this program sets the parameters and collects what each state is. BIGSTICK (github.com/cwjsdsu/BigstickPublick) gives the same energies, spins and basis dimensions: lib/nuclear/shell/bigstick_compare.py runs both.

nuclear.skyrme_hf.description:
Give it a nucleus whose protons and neutrons both fill whole shells, such as
`"16O"`, `"40Ca"`, `"48Ca"`, `"56Ni"`, `"90Zr"`, `"132Sn"` or `"208Pb"`, and a
Skyrme force. It returns the self-consistent mean-field ground state: the
total energy and the energy per nucleon, the proton, neutron and charge
radii, the energy of every occupied orbital with its name (`"n 3p1/2"`), the
other bound orbitals of the final mean field, and the densities on the
radial mesh.

This is the textbook calculation of nuclear structure (Vautherin and Brink,
1972): each nucleon moves in a field made by all the others, and the
equations are solved until the field and the orbitals agree. Lead-208 takes
about 0.09 s on 186 mesh points.

It does not do open-shell nuclei. A nucleus whose last orbital would be
partly filled, such as calcium-44, is refused with the name of that orbital:
treating it needs pairing (BCS or Hartree-Fock-Bogoliubov), which this
solver does not have.
nuclear.skyrme_hf.example:
import vipyr as vp
r = vp.nuclear.skyrme_hf()             # oxygen-16 with SLy5
print(r.e_per_a, r.r_ch, r.levels)
assert r.check()

import vipyr as vp
r = vp.nuclear.skyrme_hf()             # oxygen-16 with SLy5

import vipyr as vp

for force in ["SLy4", "SLy5", "SIII", "SkM*"]:
    a = vp.nuclear.skyrme_hf(nucleus="208Pb", force=force, spacing=0.1)

nuclear.skyrme_hf.name: skyrme_hf
nuclear.skyrme_hf.notes_md:
### The energy functional

The energy is the integral of a local density
$E = \int \mathcal{H}(\mathbf r)\, d^3 r$ built from three densities of each
kind of nucleon $q \in \{n, p\}$: the number density $\rho_q$, the
kinetic-energy density $\tau_q$ and the spin-orbit density $J_q$. Without a
subscript, $\rho = \rho_n + \rho_p$ and likewise for $\tau$ and $J$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal H ={}& \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\Big(1 - \frac1A\Big)\tau
 + \frac{t_0}{2}\Big[\Big(1 + \frac{x_0}{2}\Big)\rho^2 - \Big(x_0 + \frac12\Big)\sum_q \rho_q^2\Big] \\
&+ \frac{t_1}{4}\Big[\Big(1 + \frac{x_1}{2}\Big)\Big(\rho\tau + \frac34 (\nabla\rho)^2\Big) - \Big(x_1 + \frac12\Big)\sum_q\Big(\rho_q\tau_q + \frac34 (\nabla\rho_q)^2\Big)\Big] \\
&+ \frac{t_2}{4}\Big[\Big(1 + \frac{x_2}{2}\Big)\Big(\rho\tau - \frac14 (\nabla\rho)^2\Big) + \Big(x_2 + \frac12\Big)\sum_q\Big(\rho_q\tau_q - \frac14 (\nabla\rho_q)^2\Big)\Big] \\
&+ \frac{t_3}{12}\rho^\alpha\Big[\Big(1 + \frac{x_3}{2}\Big)\rho^2 - \Big(x_3 + \frac12\Big)\sum_q \rho_q^2\Big]
 + \frac{W_0}{2}\Big(J\,\nabla\rho + \sum_q J_q\,\nabla\rho_q\Big) \\
&+ \frac{t_1 - t_2}{16}\sum_q J_q^2 - \frac{t_1 x_1 + t_2 x_2}{16} J^2
 + \frac{e^2}{2}\rho_p(\mathbf r)\int\frac{\rho_p(\mathbf r')}{|\mathbf r - \mathbf r'|}d^3r'
 - \frac34 e^2\Big(\frac3\pi\Big)^{1/3}\rho_p^{4/3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The two $J^2$ terms are kept for SLy5 and SIII and dropped for SLy4 and SkM*,
as each force was fitted (the `j2` parameter). The last two terms are the
direct Coulomb energy and its exchange in the Slater approximation. The
factor $1 - 1/A$ is the one-body center-of-mass correction, which all four
forces use; it multiplies $\hbar^2/2m$ in the energy and in the equations
below.

### The Hartree-Fock equations

For a spherical nucleus each orbital is $R_{nlj}(r)$ times a spinor
spherical harmonic, and making $E$ stationary under changes of the orbitals
gives, for $u = rR$,

$$
-\big(B_q u'\big)' + \Big[B_q\frac{l(l+1)}{r^2} + \frac{B_q'}{r} + U_q + \delta_{qp} V_C
 + \langle\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf l\rangle \frac{W_q}{r}\Big] u = \varepsilon\, u,
\qquad \langle\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf l\rangle = j(j+1) - l(l+1) - \tfrac34,
$$

with the effective mass $B_q = \hbar^2/2m^*_q$, the central field $U_q$, the
spin-orbit field $W_q$ and the Coulomb field $V_C$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
B_q ={}& \frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\Big(1 - \frac1A\Big) + \frac18\big[t_1(2 + x_1) + t_2(2 + x_2)\big]\rho
 + \frac18\big[t_2(1 + 2x_2) - t_1(1 + 2x_1)\big]\rho_q, \\
U_q ={}& t_0\Big[\Big(1 + \frac{x_0}{2}\Big)\rho - \Big(x_0 + \frac12\Big)\rho_q\Big]
 + \frac{t_1}{4}\Big[\Big(1 + \frac{x_1}{2}\Big)\Big(\tau - \frac32\Delta\rho\Big) - \Big(x_1 + \frac12\Big)\Big(\tau_q - \frac32\Delta\rho_q\Big)\Big] \\
&+ \frac{t_2}{4}\Big[\Big(1 + \frac{x_2}{2}\Big)\Big(\tau + \frac12\Delta\rho\Big) + \Big(x_2 + \frac12\Big)\Big(\tau_q + \frac12\Delta\rho_q\Big)\Big] \\
&+ \frac{t_3}{12}\Big[\Big(1 + \frac{x_3}{2}\Big)(2 + \alpha)\rho^{\alpha + 1}
 - \Big(x_3 + \frac12\Big)\big(2\rho^\alpha\rho_q + \alpha\rho^{\alpha - 1}(\rho_n^2 + \rho_p^2)\big)\Big]
 - \frac{W_0}{2}\nabla\cdot(J + J_q), \\
W_q ={}& \frac{W_0}{2}\big(\rho' + \rho_q'\big) + \frac{t_1 - t_2}{8}J_q - \frac{t_1x_1 + t_2x_2}{8}J
 \quad(\text{the } J \text{ terms only with } j2), \\
V_C ={}& e^2\int\frac{\rho_p(\mathbf r')}{|\mathbf r - \mathbf r'|}d^3r' - e^2\Big(\frac3\pi\Big)^{1/3}\rho_p^{1/3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The occupied orbitals make the densities,
$\rho_q = \sum \frac{2j + 1}{4\pi}R^2$,
$\tau_q = \sum \frac{2j + 1}{4\pi}\big[R'^2 + \frac{l(l + 1)}{r^2}R^2\big]$ and
$J_q = \sum \frac{2j + 1}{4\pi}\langle\boldsymbol\sigma\cdot\mathbf l\rangle\frac{R^2}{r}$,
the sums running over the occupied $(n, l, j)$ of kind $q$.

### Discretization

The mesh is $r_i = (i + 1)h$ for $i < \mathrm{round}(\text{box}/h)$, with
$u = 0$ at the origin and one step past the last point. The kinetic term is
written in conservative form with $B_q$ at the midpoints (past the last point
it is the free value), so each $(l, j)$ block is a symmetric tridiagonal
matrix. Derivatives of the densities and fields are centered differences
inside and second-order one-sided differences at the ends; integrals are the
trapezoid rule; the direct Coulomb potential sums the charge inside and
outside each mesh point.

Everything is second order in $h$. Halving the spacing from 0.1 fm to 0.05
fm raises E/A by 0.014 to 0.019 MeV across the seven nuclei and four forces.
For lead-208 with SLy4 the changes from 0.1 to 0.05 fm and from 0.05 to 0.025
fm are in the ratio 4.005, and the Richardson value $(4E(h/2) - E(h))/3$
from either pair agrees to $7 \times 10^{-6}$ MeV per nucleon. Run two
spacings and extrapolate when the third decimal of E/A matters.

The default box is 15 fm, or $1.2A^{1/3} + 11.5$ fm when that is wider
(18.6 fm for lead-208). Widening it to 30 fm changes E/A by less than
$2 \times 10^{-7}$ MeV for calcium-48, tin-132 and lead-208. Orbitals within
about 1 MeV of zero in the spectrum feel the box more than that.

### Solving

The iteration starts from Woods-Saxon densities (radius $1.2A^{1/3}$ fm,
diffuseness 0.6 fm) and $\tau = J = 0$. Each pass computes the fields from
the densities, builds the matrix of every block with $l \le 7$, finds the
occupied orbitals, builds new densities and mixes them with the old ones
(Pulay's mixing by default, below). It stops when the energy changes by
less than `e_tol` between passes (after at least four). With the defaults
the seven nuclei above take 22 to 32 passes with each of the four forces
(37 to 66 with `mixing="linear"`).

The loop is lib/scf/loop.viv, with this mesh as its basis, and the mixing
is the contract `mix_densities` of lib/scf/mix.viv. `mixing="pulay"` (Pulay's
mixing, the default) and `mixing="broyden"` (Johnson's modified Broyden)
combine the last `history` passes; `history` applies to those two only.
`mixing="linear"` keeps a fraction `mix` of the new densities. For calcium-40 with SLy4 at
`e_tol=1e-10` linear mixing takes 40 passes, Pulay 32 and Broyden 24
(gallery/science/plot_scf_mixers.py). Stopped there, the three differ in
$r_{ch}$ by up to $2 \times 10^{-9}$ fm, because the energy settles before
the densities do; at `e_tol=1e-13` they agree to $2 \times 10^{-13}$ fm and
$2 \times 10^{-14}$ MeV in E/A. At the defaults (`e_tol=1e-9`), oxygen-16
with SLy5 by Pulay's mixing is within $7 \times 10^{-11}$ MeV in E/A and
$1 \times 10^{-12}$ fm in $r_{ch}$ of the run to `e_tol=1e-13`; by linear
mixing, $5 \times 10^{-11}$ MeV and $1 \times 10^{-9}$ fm.

The occupation is chosen by energy. In pass 1 every bound state of
every block is found by Sturm-sequence bisection, and the $Z$ protons (and
$N$ neutrons) go into the lowest orbitals, $2j + 1$ to each. Later passes
refine each occupied orbital by inverse iteration from its previous vector,
then use Sturm counts to confirm that it is still the same state of its
block and that no empty orbital has dropped below the highest occupied one.
When either check fails the occupation is chosen again; `refills` counts
those passes. Calcium-40's $2s_{1/2}$, the second orbital of its block, is
found the same way as the first.

### Limits

- Spherical symmetry and closed shells only: no pairing and no deformation.
  A nucleus whose last proton or neutron orbital would be partly filled is
  refused with the name of that orbital. A closed $j$ subshell counts as
  closed: carbon-12 (six of each in $1s_{1/2}$ and $1p_{3/2}$) runs and
  converges, as a spherical nucleus.
- Bound orbitals only: a nucleus whose occupied orbitals reach zero energy
  (past a drip line) is refused.
- Blocks up to $l = 7$ and at most four occupied orbitals per block, which
  covers lead-208 (its $3s_{1/2}$ protons are the third of their block).
  `spectrum` lists bound orbitals within those bounds.
- The charge radius folds the proton density with a Gaussian of range 0.65
  fm, $r_{ch}^2 = r_p^2 + \tfrac32(0.65)^2$, as skyrme_rpa does; it has no
  neutron or spin-orbit contributions to the charge density.
- The constants are skyrme_rpa's: $\hbar c = 197.327053$ MeV fm, the
  nucleon mass the average of 938.27231 and 939.56563 MeV, and
  $e^2 = 1.43986$ MeV fm.

### Verification

- Against an independent numpy solver (the reference below, its constants
  set to these) for all 28 pairs of nucleus and force on meshes of 0.1 and
  0.05 fm: E/A agrees to $4 \times 10^{-14}$ MeV, the radii to
  $9 \times 10^{-13}$ fm and the occupied levels to $2 \times 10^{-11}$ MeV,
  in the same number of passes, both mixing linearly. That solver diagonalizes each block densely
  and fills shells in a prescribed order, so the agreement also checks the
  filling by energy.
- Oxygen-16 with SLy5 and `mixing="linear"` gives the bits of the
  oxygen-16 solver in lib/skyrme/skyrme.viv. Extrapolated to $h \to 0$ it gives E/A = −8.0250
  MeV and $r_{ch}$ = 2.7993 fm, against −8.0261 MeV and 2.7991 fm in the
  sample output of skyrme_rpa (Colò et al. 2013).
- The exported library, a native build and Viv's interpreter give the same
  result bits for every case in `skyrmehf.cases.json`.

M. Beiner, H. Flocard, Nguyen Van Giai and P. Quentin, Nuclear ground-state properties and self-consistent calculations with the Skyrme interaction. (I). Spherical description, Nucl. Phys. A 238, 29 (1975). SIII.
J. Bartel, P. Quentin, M. Brack, C. Guet and H.-B. Håkansson, Towards a better parametrisation of Skyrme-like effective forces: a critical study of the SkM force, Nucl. Phys. A 386, 79 (1982). SkM*.

G. Colò, L. Cao, N. Van Giai and L. Capelli, Self-consistent RPA calculations with Skyrme-type interactions: The skyrme_rpa program, Comput. Phys. Commun. 184, 142 (2013). The constants and the charge folding used here, and the oxygen-16 check.
